text: Plato’s two laws concerning the gods make Genesis 6 difficult. Yahweh is grieved in his heart, and Yahweh resolves to destroy every living thing (Genesis 6:6–7). On Plato’s accounting, then, Yahweh is moved, and Yahweh is also the cause of harm. Plato wrote the laws against gods who do evil from caprice, and Genesis gives the flood a reason: “the earth was filled with violence” (Genesis 6:11). That reason narrows the conflict with Plato’s laws, though it does not remove it. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show that the punishment is just, and if the poet can show that the one punished is made better by it. No one is made better by a flood. What Plato does not allow is grief, since to be grieved is to be changed. For Plato, a good god cannot be affected by what is below him. For Genesis, a good God is affected by what his creatures have become, and God’s grief shows how seriously he takes their corruption. Noah and Socrates also arrive at theology at different points in their building. Noah builds under God’s judgment from the beginning, to dimensions given by God (Genesis 6:14–16), and the God who gives those dimensions has looked at the world and been wounded by it. Socrates derives his city from human need, and reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated. Both Genesis and Plato’s text read inner disorder on a larger scale: Genesis moves from every imagination of the human heart to an earth filled with violence, and Socrates looks for justice written larger in a city. When the readings break off, both constructions remain unfinished, the ark waiting for its passengers and Socrates’ city waiting for its rulers.
